output.title: Attribution starts with one source field you can trust
output.body:
If you are measuring attribution, the first question is not which dashboard to buy. It is whether every lead already passes through one place where source can be recorded in a way you can trust. If the answer is no, attribution is a data-plumbing problem first, not an AI problem.

For a small business, that usually means looking at one workflow: website form, email reply, CRM entry, or sales record. Ask a simple question: when a lead becomes a customer, can you trace it back to one channel or campaign without guessing? If the answer depends on memory, a spreadsheet note, or whatever someone typed last Tuesday, the measurement is already shaky.

The practical next step is a small manual spot-check. Pick a recent handful of closed deals, look up the original trail, and compare it with what your CRM or tracking field says. A small sample will not prove the whole system is sound, but it will show whether the control is real or just decorative. Small businesses have a talent for decorative controls right up until they need them.

If the source field is blank, inconsistent, or routinely overwritten, fix the input rule before adding AI. Once source data is reliable, you can decide whether lead scoring, channel-based replies, or another automation is worth testing. Before that, the model would only help you measure noise more neatly.
